claims.text: Fully plant-based kitchen: all chocolate and sweets are made with no animal products whatsoever, dairy-free and egg-free, so the risk of animal cross-contact is minimal.
Entirely vegan, organic, raw operation with no dairy, eggs, white sugar, additives or preservatives, making it a low-risk choice for vegan diners.
Menu uses plant milks (e.g. almond milk) for smoothies and chocolate drinks.

name: カフェ フロッシュ (Café Frosch)

claims.text: The kitchen is bread-focused, baking with whole-grain wheat flour and koji yeast, so wheat/gluten is pervasive; no gluten-free preparation or separation is documented.
This is an omnivore kitchen that also serves meat dishes such as a German sausage sandwich, so vegan items are prepared in a shared kitchen; no dedicated vegan-only prep area is documented.

Staff recommend that you tell them about your vegetarian/vegan needs and any potential allergies before choosing a menu so they can guide your order, and some vegetarian dishes can be modified to remove dairy/eggs.
Offers a clearly defined set of vegan dishes — a vegan aubergine burger set, vegan koji-bread and onigiri sets — with plant-based, naturally fermented bread.
Reviewers praise the vegan meals as 'fantastic' with thoughtful meal combinations.

No gluten-free protocol is published, and the standard course is wheat-heavy (stone-oven bread, vegan pizza, quiche), so cross-contact with wheat throughout the kitchen should be assumed for gluten-sensitive diners.

The kitchen is entirely vegan and farm-to-table, so there is no meat, fish, dashi or dairy on the premises to cross-contaminate dishes — a strong positive for vegans. The only animal product on offer is optional farm honey served alongside the bread, which can be declined.
Because lunch is reservation-only and tailored, staff ask that you tell them about vegan needs and any allergies when booking so the menu can be adjusted.
Fully vegan, organic kitchen using vegetables from the restaurant's own pesticide-free farm, eliminating animal cross-contact concerns.
English-speaking, accommodating owner and a reservation-based format that allows dietary needs to be communicated in advance.

name: ごはんぱん工房つぶつぶ (Gohan Pan Kobo Tsubutsubu)

claims.text: Not gluten-free: every bread is made with wheat flour (rice is kneaded in alongside the wheat), so gluten is present throughout the kitchen.
The facility also produces items containing eggs, dairy, peanuts, and honey, so there is cross-contamination risk for strictly plant-based diners.
Breads containing eggs or dairy are clearly labeled, helping customers avoid animal products and choose plant-based alternatives.
The base bread is plant-based, using soy milk and rice oil instead of eggs and dairy; many items are free of eggs, dairy, and honey.
Listed on a vegan/ethical directory as a bakery with many egg-, dairy-, and honey-free items that welcomes plant-based customers.
Not a gluten-free kitchen; wheat-based noodles and pasta are central to the menu and one gluten-free diner could not eat any of the savory options.

The café cooks without eggs, dairy or other animal ingredients, so animal cross-contact is inherently low; the main non-vegan exception is honey in a few dressings, which is clearly marked on the menu.
Staff offer an English menu and have been praised for explaining dishes and their ingredients in English.
Fully plant-based menu means a vegan diner can order almost anything (just avoiding the honey-marked items), with low risk of animal cross-contact.
Café of an established Kyoto sesame-oil maker with an attached shop of vetted ingredients, emphasizing food safety and seasonal local vegetables.

name: 発酵食堂カモシカ (Hakkō Shokudō Kamoshika (Fermented Food )

claims.text: Traditional Japanese soy sauce and miso (core to this kitchen) typically contain wheat; no GF accommodation is published, so gluten cross-contact via seasonings should be assumed.
The house brown-rice amazake dressing ingredient list includes 醤油 (soy sauce); there is no indication it is a wheat-free tamari, so it should be assumed to contain wheat.

This is an omnivore kitchen: the signature set meal includes mackerel heshiko, pufferfish nukazuke, and fish-sauce konjac, so fish is handled in the same kitchen as plant-based dishes. White miso soup may use a fish (bonito) dashi — confirm it is kombu-only.

Strong focus on traditional, additive-free fermented seasonings (naturally brewed soy sauce, miso, mirin, house-made koji and brown-rice amazake), and clearly identified vegan/plant-based items such as the brown-rice amazake dressing, koji-natto with fried tofu, and vegetable nukazuke.
Fucha courses include seasoned tempura, deep-fried in wheat-flour batter; no dedicated gluten-free fryer is documented, so shared frying oil is likely.
No wheat-free soy sauce (tamari) is advertised; standard Japanese shoyu used in shojin/fucha cooking typically contains wheat. Confirm at booking if gluten is a concern.
As a dedicated Buddhist fucha/shojin kitchen, the menu is plant-based by tradition with no meat, fish, eggs or dairy prepared on site, greatly reducing animal cross-contact.
Some traditional shojin kitchens use bonito-based dashi unless kombu-only stock is requested; vegans should confirm the dashi when reserving.
The restaurant's listing advises diners to tell staff about vegetarian/vegan requirements and any allergies so the menu can be chosen accordingly, indicating willingness to accommodate stated needs.
Fully plant-based Buddhist temple cuisine: no meat, fish, shellfish, dairy, eggs or honey by tradition, so no risk of animal-protein contamination from a mixed menu.
Reservation-only (by 5pm the prior day) means the kitchen can prepare for your dietary needs in advance rather than improvising on the spot.

name: インド食堂TADKA（タルカ） (Indo Shokudo TADKA (Tadka))

claims.text: The kitchen also prepares non-vegetarian dishes (especially at the TADKA2 dinner location), so shared cookware/cross-contact is possible; vegan diners should specify dairy-free and meat-free preparation.
Reviewers report the standard menu is vegetarian and that the kitchen will accommodate vegan requests when asked, but no formal allergy protocol is published.
The standard daily VEG MEALS set is built from beans and vegetables only (about 9 items), making it an easy, largely plant-based default.
Much of the South Indian repertoire (rice, sambar, rasam, chutney) is naturally wheat-free and based on rice and lentils.
